terms.grammar: aequum, neuter of aequus, as the object of facere: “you are not doing what is fair”
evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 1.2.11: tū dīs nec rēctē dīcis: nōn aequum facis (Lewis & Short), s.v. neque

terms.gloss: I accept that, I’m content with it
terms.grammar: aequī, genitive of value, with facere: “I count it as fair”
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 3.1.189: aequī istuc faciam, it will be all the same to me (Lewis & Short), s.v. aequus
terms.comment: Traupman gives it for “I think that’s fair”. In Plautus and Cicero aequī (bonīque) facere is to take a thing in good part, to be content with it, rather than to judge it fair.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 98, checked against the searchable text and the page image (12 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
